client: Lately, I’ve been so anxious about failing those two exams last semester. I keep worrying that I won’t be able to catch up, and it’s making me question whether I’ll even graduate on time. I’m not sure if talking about it will really help—it feels like the problem is just there, no matter what.
therapist: It sounds like those exams have been weighing heavily on your mind, and it’s understandable to feel anxious when something so important feels uncertain. Let’s explore this together—what thoughts come up when you think about catching up and graduating on time?

client: I keep thinking about how far behind I am, and it feels overwhelming. I worry that even if I try my hardest, I won’t be able to catch up, and I’ll end up disappointing everyone, especially my family. It’s like this constant pressure that makes it hard to even focus on studying.
therapist: It sounds like the pressure you’re feeling is not just about academics but also tied to the fear of letting others down, which can make it even harder to focus. What do you think might happen if you allowed yourself to take small, manageable steps instead of trying to tackle everything at once?

client: I guess the idea of small steps makes sense logically, but when I think about actually doing it, I panic that it won't be enough. My parents expect straight A's, and if I don't meet that standard all at once, I feel like I'm already failing them. The guilt just overwhelms me before I even start.
therapist: That guilt sounds like it's carrying so much weight for you, almost as if your worth is tangled up in those perfect grades. I wonder what it might feel like to separate your parents' expectations from your own sense of progress for a moment—how would you define "enough" for yourself right now?

client:
Honestly, the idea of separating my parents' expectations from my own progress feels impossible. Every time I get a B, I hear my dad's voice saying "Is this really your best?" in my head. Even if I tell myself it's fine, the guilt creeps in like I'm letting them down. 

How am I supposed to define "enough" when their approval has always been the measuring stick? It’s like my brain refuses to believe my own standards could matter as much.
therapist: It sounds like your dad's voice has become so ingrained that it's hard to distinguish where his expectations end and your own begin—that must feel exhausting to carry. What might it look like to gently challenge that voice by asking, "What would *compassion* sound like in this moment?"

client:
I get what you're saying about compassion, but honestly, the idea of being kind to myself just makes me feel guilty. Like if I'm not constantly pushing myself, I'm failing or being lazy. My dad always said self-compassion was just an excuse for weakness. 

It's exhausting, yeah, but I don't know how to separate that voice from what I actually believe anymore. When I try to be gentle with myself, it just feels wrong, like I'm betraying some unspoken rule.
therapist: It sounds like your dad’s perspective on self-compassion has become so deeply rooted that even considering kindness toward yourself feels like breaking a rule you’ve internalized. I wonder what it might feel like to explore small moments where you could gently question that rule—like asking, "What would it mean to see self-compassion as strength, not weakness?"

client:
I get what you're saying, but it's like... whenever I try to be kinder to myself, I immediately hear my dad's voice in my head saying I'm being lazy or making excuses. Even thinking about self-compassion makes me feel guilty, like I'm betraying how he raised me. 

I don't know if I can just flip a switch and see it as strength when my whole life I've been taught the opposite. It feels like going against everything that's kept me disciplined and successful so far.
therapist: It makes complete sense that this feels so conflicting—when self-criticism has been your motivator for so long, shifting that mindset can feel like losing your compass. What if we explored this slowly—where might there be one tiny area where you could experiment with self-kindness without it feeling like you’re abandoning discipline entirely?

client: I get what you're saying, but the idea of being kind to myself just makes me anxious. Like if I go easy on myself even a little, I'm worried I'll completely lose all my productivity and just become lazy. That critical voice in my head is the only thing that keeps me going sometimes.
therapist: It sounds like that critical voice feels like a safety net—like without it, you worry you might lose all momentum, which is understandably scary. What if we explored how productivity and self-kindness might coexist, rather than seeing them as opposites?

client:
I get what you're saying about productivity and self-kindness coexisting, but it's hard to imagine. When I try to be kinder to myself, it just feels like I'm making excuses to be lazy. The critical voice is what's kept me from completely falling apart all these years. 

I worry that if I let up even a little, everything will start slipping through my fingers. Maybe that sounds extreme, but that's how it feels.
therapist: It makes sense that this fear feels so real—when that critical voice has been your anchor for so long, the idea of loosening its grip can feel like risking everything. What if we gently explored what "slipping through your fingers" actually looks like in reality, rather than in your fears?

client: I guess the fear is that if I stop being so hard on myself, I'll become lazy or make huge mistakes. It's like this voice in my head is the only thing keeping me from falling apart. But when you put it that way, it does sound kind of extreme—like I'm either perfect or a complete failure, with no in-between.
therapist: It sounds like you’re starting to notice how black-and-white that thinking can be—either perfect or a failure—which is such an important insight. What might it feel like to explore what the "in-between" could look like for you, even just a little?

client: I get what you're saying about the in-between, but it's hard to imagine. When I mess up even a little at work, it feels like the whole project is ruined. The idea of "good enough" just makes me anxious—like I'm settling for less than I should be.
therapist: It sounds like "good enough" feels like a slippery slope toward failure, which can make it incredibly hard to embrace any middle ground. What might happen if we explored what "good enough" could look like in a way that still feels aligned with your values and goals, rather than a compromise?
